newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON PROVES MAN CAN BE BIGGER THAN HIS SPORT.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON PROVES MAN CAN BE BIGGER THAN HIS SPORT.

text.p: For the second time in two years, Michael Johnson seems intent on proving the sport is not necessarily bigger than the man.
Last year the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) juggled the Olympic schedule to allow Johnson to attempt a 200-400 metres double at the Atlanta Games.
Johnson duly delivered, capping his performance with 19.32 astounding seconds during which he sent the world 200 metres record spinning into another dimension.
This year, the IAAF again bent over backwards to accommodate the Texan after injury prevented him from competing in the U.S. trials.
Desperate to have the sport's biggest attraction appear at the sixth world championships starting on Saturday, the IAAF decided to award wild card entries to all defending champions.

The harsh winner-takes-all principle underlying the American championships, by which the first three only qualify for a world championships or Olympic Games, was thereby neatly circumvented and Johnson will line up in the 400 metres here.
An appropriate reward for the world governing body at the first outdoor world championships to offer prize money and world record bonuses would be a world record in the one-lap sprint.

If successful, Johnson would become the first man to hold both the 200 and 400 marks and would also be $160,000 better off after collecting $60,000 for finishing first and a bonus of $100,000 for breaking the world record.

Johnson's current form remains a mystery and although he has the year's fastest time of 43.75 seconds it was set back in April before he injured his left quadriceps in the heavily hyped but somewhat hollow 150 metres showdown with Olympic 100 champion Donovan Bailey.
Bailey may need to improve his world mark of 9.84 seconds set in Atlanta last year to repel the challenge of Ato Boldon and Maurice Greene.
Both men are coached in California by John Smith, who believes the world record should be closer to 9.7 seconds than 9.8.
Wilson Kipketer, the gifted Kenyan who now runs for Denmark, is another runner who could go home with a world record.

As he showed by breaking the world 800 metres best twice at the Paris world indoor championships last March, Kipketer does not need pacemakers. This month he equalled Seb Coe's 16-year-old outdoor record of one minute 41.73 seconds after seemingly showing no interest during the first 400 metres.
"I want to break the world record," Kipketer said. "But it depends on many things like the weather. If the weather is hot it will become far more difficult.
"I will try my best for a world record in Athens but I will not be the only man running the 800 metres."
No record is anticipated in the 1,500 which promises instead a fascinating tactical battle between three times champion Noureddine Morceli and the young pretender Hicham el Guerrouj.

Daniel Komen, who failed to make the Kenyan team for Atlanta, has a point to prove in the 5,000 and the field events feature Cuban long jumper Ivan Pedroso, who plans to extend the world record past nine metres some time soon.
Marion Jones, the American sprinter and long jumper, has awesome potential if rudimentary technique.
But only Olympic 100 champion Gail Devers has run faster this year, beating Jones by one hundredth of a second on a rain-soaked evening in Lausanne.
The 100 metres will also feature Merlene Ottey, the 37-year-old Jamaican who has won a record 13 world medals.
Ottey, who defends her 200 title here as well, told reporters on Thursday: "A month ago I thought I would only run the 100 metres because I wasn't feeling all that good.
"I was sick then I had trouble with a hamstring and then with my ankle, so it's been a struggle but now I'm okay and hopefully I will be able to produce my best."
For the first time since the inaugural 1983 Helsinki championships there is no Carl Lewis and there is no Linford Christie either to take on the Americans.
In Jones, though, the latest edition of the world championships may have an athlete fit to rank with any in the history of track and field.
